query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (~5 at.%) of tin (Sn) into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (by doping the melt to achieve a Sn-doped alloy) will promote the formation of a continuous, Sn‐enriched interfacial layer during high‐temperature oxidation. This Sn-rich layer will act as a barrier to oxygen diffusion and suppress pest oxidation and scale spallation, thereby improving the alloy’s oxygen resistance without degrading its room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but showing rapid oxidation in air.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 at.% Sn into the alloy composition (by partial substitution or as an additive during melting) while maintaining the overall equiatomic balance of the five principal elements.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at temperatures from 800 °C up to 1000 °C; exposure times ranging from short-term (5 h) to long-term (up to 100–200 h); mechanical load conditions typical for tensile and compressive testing at room temperature and at 1000 °C (strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) without introducing service-level cyclic stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective, Sn-rich interfacial layer (potentially involving intermetallic compounds such as Nb3Sn or similar phases) at the scale/alloy interface.
generation.mechanism: The Sn dopant is expected to segregate during oxidation to form a continuous interfacial layer that alters the oxidation pathway. By promoting the formation of stable Sn-related intermetallic phases, the diffusion of oxygen into the substrate is inhibited and the violent pesting behavior (rapid, catastrophic oxidation) is suppressed. This mechanism is analogous to reports in Nb-silicide systems where Sn additions improve scale adhesion and lower oxidation kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Sn-doped version will show a significantly reduced oxidation weight gain, delayed or suppressed onset of pest oxidation, and reduced spallation of the oxide scale, while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy suffers from rapid oxygen ingress and pest oxidation during air exposure at high temperatures (e.g., 800 °C), despite its promising mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable to cast, equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloys under static oxidation tests in air at 800–1000 °C and under low to moderate mechanical strain (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹). The effect is not guaranteed if service conditions involve aggressive mechanical cycling or different atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: While the beneficial effects of Sn on oxidation resistance have been demonstrated in Nb-silicide and related refractory alloys (see PMC6981790 and PMC8715753), its impact when applied to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is unverified. It is uncertain whether the phase stability and mechanical performance of the equiatomic system will remain unaltered by a Sn addition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one standard cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another with an additional ~5 at.% Sn (adjusted by substitution to maintain total composition). Subject both to identical isothermal oxidation tests in air at 800 °C and 1000 °C for various durations (e.g., 5 h, 50 h, and 100 h). In parallel, perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength measurements under strain rates of 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻² s⁻¹.
measurements: Scale morphology and adhesion (via SEM and XRD)
Phase composition at the scale/alloy interface (via TEM/EDS)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% lower weight gain and improved scale adhesion with minimal spallation) in oxidation compared to the untreated alloy, or if its mechanical properties degrade beyond acceptable limits, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. This research was motivated by the need to understand how Sn improves the oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys. We discussed the selection of the Sn concentration in Nb-silicide based alloys of the Nb-Ti-Si-Al-Cr-Sn system and presented the results of a systematic study of three alloys of nominal compositions, namely Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Cr-5Sn (ZX4), Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Sn (ZX6), and Nb-24Ti-18Si-5Al-5Cr-5Sn (ZX8). There was macrosegregation in all three alloys that was most severe in ZX8. The Nbss was not stable in ZX6, the Nb3Sn was stable in all three alloys and the Nbss and the C14-NbCr2 Laves phase were stable in ZX4 and ZX8. In all three alloys, the primary βNb5Si3 transformed completely to αNb5Si3 after heat treatment.
